articles.title: Icahn’s Fortune Sinks to $1.3b as Debt Pressures Rise
articles.description: Carl Icahn’s fortune has dwindled to about $1.3 billion as mounting debt squeezes his business empire, leaving the longtime corporate raider and activist investor facing one of the toughest stretches of his career. When Icahn Enterprises reported third-quarter earnings this month, it warned there was no assurance it could refinance $1.4 billion of bonds due in May on acceptable terms — or at all. Since then, the pressure has only intensified. Shares of CVR Energy, a key IEP holding, have tumbled about 40% since it agreed earlier this month to buy two additional refineries, eroding the value of a stake that accounted for about half of Icahn’s publicly traded investment partnership at the end of September. Yields on some of IEP’s 2029 bonds now exceed 30%, and the company has about $4.4 billion of bonds outstanding. Tom Maloney, Bloomberg News Editor, discusses how lots of leverage of led to Carl Icahn's investment losses. (Source: Bloomberg)

articles.title: When the unthinkable happens: perceptions of monetary policy in tail events
articles.description: Focus Public perceptions of monetary policy play a central role in determining the effectiveness of policy actions. Despite central banks’ efforts to improve communication, the public has an incomplete understanding of how policymakers respond to economic shocks. This challenge becomes particularly acute during rare and severe shocks, or “tail events”, that fall outside past experience. In such circumstances, misperceptions about monetary policy can amplify economic fluctuations and undermine stabilisation efforts. In this paper we examine how public perceptions of monetary policy evolve following tail events and whether misperceptions can amplify and propagate their macroeconomic effects. Contribution We develop a dynamic stochastic general equilibrium model in which private agents – households and firms – have incomplete information about both the central bank’s response to inflation and the distribution of economic shocks. They simultaneously learn about monetary policy and the nature of shocks by observing economic outcomes. We examine how this learning process shapes inflation and output dynamics following large adverse oil supply shocks. We also test the relevance of this process using US data, estimating a nonlinear vector autoregression model with exogenous variables in which the effects of oil supply shocks depend on their size. This enables us to compare how small and large shocks affect views about monetary policy responsiveness, inflation expectations and macroeconomic outcomes. Findings We find that large adverse supply shocks lead private agents to underestimate how strongly the central bank responds to inflation. Because such shocks are rare, agents initially underestimate their likelihood and interpret part of the resulting inflation increase as evidence of a weaker monetary policy response. These misperceptions raise inflation expectations, generating persistent inflation and a temporary increase in output above its usual level. This is especially the case following large shocks, while small shocks have limited effects on agents’ beliefs. Evidence from US data supports these findings, showing that large oil supply shocks are associated with lower perceptions of monetary policy responsiveness, persistent inflation expectations and output overshooting. Our findings highlight the importance of central bank communication and credibility in stabilising expectations during tail events. ______________________________________________________________________ For webstaging purposes, please add: Abstract We study how public perceptions of monetary policy evolve when the economy experiences rare and severe supply shocks. When agents learn in real time about the distribution of the shocks and the monetary policy reaction function, they tend to underestimate the strength of the response to inflation following large but infrequent negative supply shocks. Embedding this mechanism in a general equilibrium model with learning, we show that it endogenously generates inflation dynamics persistently above target and temporary output overshooting after a tail event. Using U.S. data, we find empirical evidence supporting our model's predictions about the distinctive role of tail events in shaping policy perceptions and macroeconomic dynamics. Our findings indicate that public misperceptions can amplify and prolong the aggregate effects of tail events, potentially undermining central banks' stabilization efforts.
